title: Development — Chapter Summary
intro: What does it mean for a person, a state or a country to be DEVELOPED? Different people have different — sometimes conflicting — answers. Income matters, but so do equality, health, education, environment, freedom and security. This chapter teaches how to compare countries on per capita income, why income alone is not enough, why public facilities matter for the poor, what the Human Development Index measures, and why all development must be SUSTAINABLE.

branches.label: Comparing countries
details: World Bank: high / middle / low income

sections.heading: Different People, Different Development Goals
bullets: Different people have different and even conflicting development goals.
What is development for one (a dam) may be destruction for another (displaced adivasi).
Goals mix MONEY with NON-MATERIAL things — freedom, equal treatment, security, respect.
Even rich people want safety, dignity and a clean environment.

sections.heading: Comparing Countries — Per Capita Income
bullets: Total income depends on population — useless for comparison.
Per capita income = total income ÷ population.
World Bank classifies countries as HIGH-INCOME, MIDDLE-INCOME or LOW-INCOME.
India is in the LOW-MIDDLE income group.

sections.heading: Beyond Income — Public Facilities
bullets: Average income hides INEQUALITY.
Some things cannot be bought directly — they need PUBLIC FACILITIES (schools, health centres, water, electricity).
Public facilities matter most for the POOR who cannot afford private alternatives.
Indicators beyond income: IMR, literacy rate, net attendance, life expectancy.

sections.heading: Indian States — Kerala vs Haryana
bullets: Haryana has higher per capita income than Kerala.
Kerala has lower IMR, higher literacy, higher net attendance.
Why? Better PUBLIC HEALTH and PUBLIC EDUCATION in Kerala.
Income matters, but how it is spent matters more.

sections.heading: Human Development Index
bullets: Published yearly by the UNDP in the Human Development Report.
Combines three dimensions: per capita income, life expectancy at birth, education (years of schooling).
HDI value lies between 0 and 1.
India is in the medium-human-development band; Sri Lanka has a higher HDI than India.
The HDI captures life-quality, not income alone.

sections.heading: Sustainability of Development
bullets: Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising future generations.
Groundwater is being pumped faster than rains can refill it (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan).
World crude oil reserves last about 35–40 years at current rates.
Reckless deforestation reduces rainfall, biodiversity and increases erosion.
Climate change crosses national borders; countries must cooperate.

key_takeaways: Development means different things to different people — income + non-material goals.
Per capita income (average) helps compare countries; World Bank groups: high / middle / low.
Income alone hides inequality and ignores public goods.
Public facilities — schools, health centres, water, electricity — matter most for the poor.
Indian indicators: IMR, literacy, net attendance, life expectancy show that Kerala (lower PCI) does better than Haryana on human development.
UNDP's HDI combines per capita income, life expectancy and education.
Sustainable development is essential — groundwater, oil, forests must be used carefully.
Environmental issues cross borders; countries must cooperate on climate.

glossary.definition: Improvement in the quality of life of a person, state or country — through income and non-material goals.
Total income of a country divided by its population; the average income per person.
An international institution that classifies countries by per capita income (high / middle / low) in its World Development Reports.
A service provided collectively by the government — public school, hospital, water supply, electricity, transport.
Goods that benefit everyone and cannot easily be sold individually — clean air, public parks, street lighting.
The number of children that die before the age of one year per 1000 live births in a year.
The proportion of the population aged 7 years and above that is literate.
Children aged 6–10 attending school as a percentage of all children of that age group.
The average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth.
A composite UNDP index combining per capita income, life expectancy and education on a 0–1 scale.
United Nations Development Programme — the UN body that publishes the Human Development Report.
Development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own.
Water that has soaked into the soil and rock and lies under the ground in aquifers; pumped by tube-wells.
A resource (like crude oil or coal) that takes millions of years to form and is being used up far faster.
Differences in income, wealth, opportunity or access to public goods between groups in a society.
